title: Volunteers’ Perspectives on Mental Health and Care Coordination for People Experiencing Homelessness: A Qualitative Focus Group Study
content: Background/Objectives: Coordinating voluntary outreach with formal services requires understanding volunteers’ accounts of role boundaries, unmet support needs, and barriers to continuity of care. This study explored volunteers’ perceptions of mental health needs, barriers to health and social care, and support resources in León, Spain. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study used two semi-structured focus groups with nine volunteers from a humanitarian nongovernmental organisation. Sessions were audio- and video-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed using a general inductive approach. Reporting was guided by COREQ. Results: Two themes and seven subthemes were identified. Volunteers described perceived mental health difficulties, deterioration, substance use, stigma, fragmented access to services, and limited continuity after hospital discharge. They highlighted the reduced visibility of women experiencing homelessness and concerns about their safety. Sustained accompaniment and informal relationships were valued, but participants reported uncertainty about role boundaries, gaps in training, and limited access to professional support. Their accounts described volunteering as both meaningful and emotionally demanding and revealed a tension between requests for training and participation in available sessions. Conclusions: The findings identify context-specific priorities for coordinating voluntary outreach with health, social care, and housing services. For nursing management, they suggest areas for collaborative service development: clear referral and discharge pathways, defined responsibilities, accessible training, and support for emotionally demanding outreach. These proposals require evaluation; the study did not measure quality of life, burnout, or service effectiveness.
